messages.content: Write the introduction to a monthly engineering newsletter whose theme this month is technical debt. Around 200 words.

Nobody sits down on a Tuesday and decides to make the codebase worse.

That's the awkward thing about technical debt: almost every piece of it was a reasonable call at the time. Ship before the demo. Copy the config instead of refactoring the loader. Leave the TODO, because the sprint ends Friday and the thing works. Each decision is defensible on its own. It's the compound interest that gets you — the fourth engineer who has to read the copied config, the outage nobody could diagnose because the logging was "temporary" in 2023.

This month we're not doing the usual sermon about paying it down. We're asking a harder question: which debt is worth keeping?

Because some of it is. A hacky script that runs twice a year and has never failed is not a crisis, it's a script. The real cost isn't messiness, it's the tax on change — how much slower does this code make the next person who touches it?

Inside: a walkthrough of the auth service rewrite (and why we stopped halfway), a rough method for scoring debt by blast radius rather than ugliness, and one team's argument for deliberately writing code they know they'll throw away.

Read on. Bring receipts.
